claims.text: The target high-entropy alloys may contain latent chemical ordering despite initially being treated as random solid solutions.
A DFT-plus-Monte Carlo simulation can explicitly model the evolution of chemical short-range order in these alloys.
Chemical short-range ordering produces HfTi clustering.
Chemical short-range ordering produces TiZr clustering.
HfTi and TiZr clustering establishes percolation pathways within the alloy.
The resulting clusters and percolation networks locally alter phonon-scattering processes.
The altered phonon-scattering processes lower phonon thermal conductivity.
Explicitly modeling chemical short-range order provides a more realistic description of phonon interactions than homogenized random-alloy models.
The proposed framework will predict low phonon thermal conductivity more accurately than models that assume a random alloy state.
Accounting for chemical short-range order may reduce thermal-conductivity prediction error by more than 20% relative to conventional models.
The approach is primarily applicable to high-entropy alloys containing sufficient concentrations of Hf, Ti, and Zr for short-range ordering to occur.
The approach may lose accuracy in alloys lacking Hf, Ti, or Zr.
The approach may lose accuracy in regimes where long-range order dominates microstructural effects.
Varying Hf, Ti, and Zr contents can be used to induce or suppress chemical short-range ordering in a test series.
HfTi and TiZr clustering and percolation can be assessed using TEM or atom-probe tomography.
Phonon thermal conductivity can be experimentally benchmarked using laser-flash analysis or time-domain thermoreflectance.
Failure to exceed a 20% error reduction over a conventional model in clearly clustered samples is specified as a falsifying outcome.
Absence of the expected short-range order in alloys predicted to have low thermal conductivity is specified as a falsifying outcome.
